title: Newcastle plan adjustment to traditional black-and-white-striped home kit
content:
Newcastle United are planning a deviation from their traditional block black-and-white-striped shirt for their home kit next season.

In 2026-27, Eddie Howe’s side will wear shirts with a mixture of different-sized black stripes, some of which run through the larger white stripes, with a thicker one down the middle of the front, and with a blue trim. The black which features on the largely white sleeves will be pin stripes.

This is not the first time Newcastle have reimagined the block monochrome lines. The famous “barcode” shirt between 1990 and 1993, which featured thicker stripes on one half and thinner stripes on the other, appears to have partly inspired next season’s kit. The 2021-22 shirt, meanwhile, featured only one black stripe down the middle, flanked by white on either side and black on the sleeves.

But a design which has been circulated on social media in recent weeks shows a fresh conceptualisation of the famous black-and-white stripes. While the images are not of the actual prospective kit, The Athletic has learned that they are largely representative of how the shirt will look.

How the innovative amendment of the black-and-white stripes is received among Newcastle fans remain to be seen, although the kit itself is still clearly identifiable as the club’s iconic colours, albeit in a new form.

Newcastle have worn black-and-white-striped kits since 1894, having spent two years in red shirts and white shorts following the merger between Newcastle East End and Newcastle West End in 1892.

Adidas, who returned as the club’s kit manufacturer last season, are producing the new strip, and it remains to be seen who the front-of-shirt sponsor will be, given the present deal with SELA is up at the end of the season. Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF), Newcastle’s majority owners, own SELA, an entertainment and hospitality company.

Newcastle’s kit deal with Adidas is worth somewhere between £25million ($33.7m) and £40m annually, a significant increase on the £6m per year they were previously receiving from Castore.

The Athletic have approached Newcastle for comment.

New kits always engender much intrigue and enthusiasm from supporters — and often a fresh design, at least initially, is not particularly well received among the wider fanbase.

There is likely to be an even greater negative reaction than normal to Newcastle’s proposed shirt for 2026-27, given that it does represent a clear departure from the traditional block black-and-white stripes.

While traditionalists may not be receptive to attempts to reimagine the a shirt which is globally recognisable as Newcastle’s, this is not the first and nor will it be the last time that a kit is released which splits opinion.

Those inside the club are willing to be innovative as they search for increased revenues and, while it is debatable whether a move away from monochrome block stripes will dramatically alter their income streams, clearly Newcastle are gong to push boundaries as they aim to close the gap to the elite clubs.

Come August when Newcastle are playing in the new kit, even if some fans do not like the design, many will still buy it and they will support the players who are wearing it on the pitch.
